title: Mathlib Imports
content: Imports the core Mathlib libraries for natural numbers, integers, real numbers, and general tactics. These provide the floor function $\lfloor \cdot \rfloor$, the real exponentiation $\alpha^n$, and the Finset API needed to formalize sums of distinct elements.
mathContext: The floor function $\lfloor x \rfloor : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and Finset summation $\sum_{s \in T} s$ are the key primitives from Mathlib used throughout this formalization.

title: Additive Completeness
content: A set $S \subset \mathbb{Z}$ is additively complete if all sufficiently large integers can be represented as sums of distinct elements from $S$. This generalizes the classical notion of a complete sequence from additive number theory, where the representation must use distinct terms.
mathContext: $S$ is **additively complete** if $\exists N \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $\forall m \geq N$, there exists a finite subset $T \subseteq S$ with all elements distinct and $\sum_{t \in T} t = m$. The key distinction from bases of finite order (as in Waring's problem) is that elements may not be repeated.

title: Exponential Floor Sequence
content: Defines the exponential floor sequence $a_n = \lfloor t\alpha^n \rfloor$ for parameters $t, \alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This sequence grows exponentially when $\alpha > 1$, and its completeness properties depend delicately on both $t$ and $\alpha$.
mathContext: The sequence $\{\lfloor t\alpha^n \rfloor\}_{n=0}^{\infty}$ interpolates between polynomial-like behavior (when $\alpha$ is close to 1) and extremely lacunary behavior (when $\alpha$ is large). The growth rate $\alpha$ controls whether consecutive terms leave gaps too large to fill by sums of earlier terms.

title: Good Pair (t, α)
content: A pair $(t, \alpha)$ is 'good' if the exponential floor sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n \rfloor$ is additively complete. The central problem is to characterize the set of all good pairs in the positive quadrant $(0,\infty) \times (0,\infty)$.
mathContext: Define $\mathcal{G} = \{(t,\alpha) \in (0,\infty)^2 : \{\lfloor t\alpha^n \rfloor\}_{n \geq 0} \text{ is complete}\}$. Problem #349 asks for a description of $\mathcal{G}$. Graham's work shows $\mathcal{G}$ has a surprisingly intricate structure even for fixed $t$.

title: Erdős Problem #349: Characterization
content: The main open problem: characterize all pairs $(t, \alpha)$ with $t > 0, \alpha > 0$ for which $\lfloor t\alpha^n \rfloor$ is a complete sequence. This is stated as an axiom since the problem remains open — the characterization set $S$ exists but its exact description is unknown.
mathContext: The axiom asserts $\exists S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ such that $\forall t, \alpha > 0$: $(t,\alpha) \in S \iff \lfloor t\alpha^n \rfloor$ is complete. The deep question is **what $S$ looks like** — whether it has a clean characterization or is inherently complex (as Graham's result suggests).

title: Golden Ratio Conjecture
content: The central conjecture: $\lfloor t\alpha^n \rfloor$ is complete for all $t > 0$ and $1 < \alpha < \varphi$, where $\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2 \approx 1.618$ is the golden ratio. The golden ratio threshold arises because it is the growth rate of the Fibonacci sequence, which is the prototypical complete sequence with exponential growth.
mathContext: The **Fibonacci sequence** $F_n$ satisfies $F_{n+1}/F_n \to \varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2$, and Zeckendorf's theorem guarantees every positive integer has a unique representation as a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers. The conjecture posits that completeness persists for all sequences growing at rate $< \varphi$, regardless of the multiplicative constant $t$.

title: Graham's Disjoint Segments Theorem
content: For any $k \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $t_k \in (0,1)$ such that the set $\{\alpha : \lfloor t_k \alpha^n \rfloor \text{ is complete}\}$ consists of at least $k$ disjoint open intervals. This 1964 result of Ronald Graham reveals the completeness region has a fractal-like complexity even for a single parameter value $t$.
mathContext: Graham proved: $\forall k \in \mathbb{N}, \exists t_k \in (0,1)$ and disjoint intervals $(a_1, b_1), \ldots, (a_k, b_k)$ such that $\alpha \in (a_i, b_i) \implies \lfloor t_k \alpha^n \rfloor$ is complete. The formalization captures this as a function from $\mathrm{Fin}\, k$ to sets of reals satisfying disjointness and the completeness property.

title: Parity: ⌊(3/2)^n⌋ Odd Infinitely Often
content: The open sub-problem: is $\lfloor (3/2)^n \rfloor$ odd for infinitely many $n$? This deceptively simple question about the parity of a specific exponential floor sequence is intimately connected to the Waring problem for powers of $3/2$ and the distribution of the fractional parts $\{(3/2)^n\}$.
mathContext: The parity of $\lfloor (3/2)^n \rfloor$ is determined by the fractional part: $\lfloor (3/2)^n \rfloor$ is odd $\iff \{(3/2)^n\} < 1/2$ (when $\lfloor (3/2)^n \rfloor$ is odd). The equidistribution of $\{(3/2)^n\}$ modulo 1 is unresolved — it is not even known whether this sequence is dense in $[0,1]$.

title: Parity: ⌊(3/2)^n⌋ Even Infinitely Often
content: The companion open problem: is $\lfloor (3/2)^n \rfloor$ even for infinitely many $n$? Together with the odd case, these parity questions represent one of the most basic unsolved problems about exponential sequences. A negative answer to either would have dramatic consequences for our understanding of $\{(3/2)^n\}$ distribution.
mathContext: If $\lfloor (3/2)^n \rfloor$ were eventually always odd (or always even), it would imply the fractional parts $\{(3/2)^n\}$ eventually avoid either $[0, 1/2)$ or $[1/2, 1)$, contradicting the expected equidistribution. This connects to Vijayaraghavan's work on the distribution of $(3/2)^n \pmod{1}$.

title: Waring-Type Connection
content: The completeness problem for $\lfloor t\alpha^n \rfloor$ connects to representation problems in additive number theory. Just as Waring's problem asks about representing integers as sums of $k$-th powers, Problem #349 asks about representation using exponentially growing sequences — but with the additional constraint that terms must be distinct.
mathContext: In Waring's problem, $g(k) = \min\{s : \forall n, n = x_1^k + \cdots + x_s^k\}$ depends critically on $\lfloor (3/2)^k \rfloor$. Specifically, $g(k) = 2^k + \lfloor (3/2)^k \rfloor - 2$ when $2^k \{(3/2)^k\} + \lfloor (3/2)^k \rfloor \leq 2^k$. This is the **Ideal Waring formula**, verified for $k \leq 471{,}600{,}000$ by Kubina–Wunderlich.
